newsitem.title: NORWAY: POLL - Norway's Progress Party makes big gains.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Norway's Progress Party makes big gains.

text.p: Barely five weeks before the Norwegian election the right-wing Progress Party is emerging as the second largest political force after the ruling Labour Party, according to an opinion poll released on Thursday.

The survey, carried out by Scanfact for daily Verdens Gang, gave Carl I. Hagen's Progress Party 23.5 percent, a rise of seven points from a similar poll in June and up 17.2 points from the 1993 election.
Verdens Gang said the survey indicated Norway could be facing a political earthquake in the September 15 election.
"The opportunistic protest-and-promise policy (of the Progress Party) has been successful among Norwegians this summer," the tabloid said.
It was the third poll this month to show the Progress Party receiving more than 20 percent of voter support.
Scanfact gave Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland's Labour Party 29.5 percent, down 0.5 points from June and down 7.4 points from the last election. The party rules in a minority government.

"But a lot will happen between now and September 15," Verdens Gang said. "We know from experience that the Labour Party will gain support in the next few weeks. Its message of creating 190,000 new jobs and keeping interest rates low will make many voters cast their ballot for Jagland, although they may wish to vote for Hagen."
Hagen told Verdens Gang: "The next few weeks are going to be tough. Everyone is out to get me now."

The three-party centrist bloc in parliament, seen as the main threat to Jagland's government, fell two points from June to a combined 23 percent. In the 1993 election, the Centre Party, Christian People's Party and the liberal Venstre polled 28.3 percent.
The Conservatives, who were the second biggest party at 17.0 percent in the 1993 election, slipped four points from the June survey, to 14.5 percent.
The poll was carried out on Wednesday among a sample of 1,000 voters.
The Labour Party, which is the biggest of the eight parties in the 165-seat Storting, or parliament, has been in power since 1990.
